Potter and Clay
POT-ter and KLAY
n. phrase
Potter: Hebrew yōtsēr (one who forms; from yātsar, to form); Greek kerameus. Clay: Hebrew chōmer (clay, mud); Greek pēlos. One of the great biblical metaphors for the LORD’s sovereign forming of His creatures, running from Isaiah and Jeremiah through Romans 9.

See also: Potter and Clay

📖 Biblical Definition

The potter-and-clay metaphor is one of the most extensive and theologically loaded in the Bible, governing the doctrine of the LORD’s sovereign forming of His creatures. The OT references are foundational. Isaiah 29:16: surely your turning of things upside down shall be esteemed as the potter’s clay: for shall the work say of him that made it, He made me not? or shall the thing framed say of him that framed it, He had no understanding? Isaiah 45:9: woe unto him that striveth with his Maker! Let the potsherd strive with the potsherds of the earth. Shall the clay say to him that fashioneth it, What makest thou? Isaiah 64:8: but now, O LORD, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand. Jeremiah 18:1-10 develops the doctrine at greatest length, with the LORD instructing Jeremiah to go down to the potter’s house and watch him work: then I went down to the potter’s house, and, behold, he wrought a work on the wheels. And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it. Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel. The supreme New Testament development is Romans 9:19-23, Paul’s defense of God’s sovereign election: thou wilt say then unto me, Why doth he yet find fault? For who hath resisted his will? Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour? What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction: And that he might make known the riches of his glory on the vessels of mercy, which he had afore prepared unto glory.... Several structural features mark the doctrine. First, the absolute sovereignty: the potter has complete authority over the clay; the clay has no claim against the potter; the question why hast thou made me thus? is forbidden as creature-against-Creator presumption. Second, the differentiation of vessels: from the same lump the potter makes vessels of various kinds—some unto honour, some unto dishonour, by his sovereign choice. Third, the application to election: the potter-and-clay imagery answers the protests against the doctrine of God’s sovereign election by establishing the comprehensive principle of Creator-over-creature authority that election presupposes. Fourth, the pastoral application: the saint is to receive his own forming by the Potter’s hand with submission, recognizing that the LORD’s purposes in his particular circumstances (gifts, limitations, providences, sufferings) are the Potter’s sovereign shaping, not arbitrary fate to be resisted but appointed forming to be embraced. The potter-and-clay doctrine therefore organizes one of the deepest theological structures in Scripture: the LORD’s absolute sovereignty over His creatures, expressed in the various vessels He forms from the same lump for the various purposes of His glory.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines POTTER as one who manufactures earthen vessels; in scripture, one of the great metaphors for the LORD’s sovereign forming of His creatures (Isa 29:16; 45:9; 64:8; Jer 18:1-10), developed by Paul in Romans 9 as the structural-doctrinal answer to protests against the sovereign election of God.

expand to see more

POTTER, n. — One who manufactures earthen vessels. In scripture, applied to the LORD as the sovereign Former of His creatures, with the various biblical references developing the metaphor across Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Romans 9.

CLAY, n. — A soft, plastic earth, used in making pottery; in scripture, the creature considered in his moldable creatureliness before the Potter’s sovereign hand.

📖 Key Scripture

Isaiah 64:8 — "But now, O LORD, thou art our father; we are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand."

Jeremiah 18:6 — "O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter? saith the LORD. Behold, as the clay is in the potter’s hand, so are ye in mine hand, O house of Israel."

Romans 9:20-21 — "Nay but, O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Shall the thing formed say to him that formed it, Why hast thou made me thus? Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?"

2 Corinthians 4:7 — "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The potter-and-clay doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the universalist-or-Arminian reading that has muted Paul’s Romans 9 use of the metaphor in defense of God’s sovereign election (reducing the potter-and-clay to general providence without the specifically-elective substance)—and on the other by the hyper-Calvinist reading that has used the metaphor to justify a deterministic-fatalist view of God’s sovereignty that loses the creaturely-responsibility dimension Scripture maintains alongside.

expand to see more

The universalist-or-Arminian reading has often muted Paul’s explicit use of the potter-and-clay metaphor in Romans 9 to defend the doctrine of God’s sovereign election. The verses are difficult; the doctrine they support is uncomfortable; the contemporary distaste for the substantive doctrine of unconditional election has often produced readings that handle the metaphor in safer general-providence terms (the potter shapes vessels for various purposes in the world; the believer should submit to God’s providence) without engaging Paul’s actual argument about the sovereign election of vessels-of-mercy and the parallel reprobation of vessels-of-wrath. The Reformed tradition has consistently insisted on the substantive Romans 9 doctrine: the potter-and-clay metaphor answers the protests against God’s sovereign election by establishing the Creator-over-creature authority that election presupposes. The recovery is the recovery of attention to Paul’s actual argument: hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?—the question itself is rhetorically settled, and the answer is the substantive doctrine of God’s sovereign election that the metaphor is deployed to defend.

The opposite corruption is the hyper-Calvinist reading that has used the metaphor to justify a deterministic-fatalist view of God’s sovereignty that loses the creaturely-responsibility dimension Scripture maintains alongside. On this reading, the clay is utterly passive; the potter does whatever He pleases without regard to the clay’s response; the saint’s responsibility for his actions disappears under the comprehensive determinism the metaphor is taken to imply. The biblical balance is more careful. The same Scripture that teaches the LORD’s absolute sovereignty teaches the creature’s real responsibility; the same Romans that asserts God’s sovereign election (chapter 9) commands the believer’s active obedience (chapter 12); the LORD’s sovereignty and the creature’s responsibility stand together throughout Scripture as compatible truths held in mystery. The potter-and-clay metaphor establishes the absolute Creator-over-creature authority that grounds election; it does not abolish the creature’s responsibility for his actions or reduce him to a passive object. Recover both ends. Refuse the muting of Romans 9’s substantive doctrine, and refuse the hyper-deterministic reading that loses creaturely responsibility. The biblical potter-and-clay doctrine is the LORD’s absolute sovereignty in election held together with the creature’s real responsibility for his response—both stand on the Scripture that asserts both, and the saint submits to the sovereign Potter who has formed him and walks in the responsible obedience the same God commands.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yōtsēr (potter) and chōmer (clay); Greek kerameus (potter) and pēlos (clay); the great biblical metaphor of the LORD’s sovereign forming of His creatures (Isa 29:16; 45:9; 64:8; Jer 18:1-10) developed by Paul in Rom 9:19-23 as the structural-doctrinal answer to protests against God’s sovereign election of vessels-of-mercy and vessels-of-wrath from the same lump.

expand to see more

Hebrew yōtsēr (H3335) — potter (participle of yātsar, to form).

Hebrew chōmer (H2563) — clay, mud (also tit, H2916).

Greek kerameus (G2763) — potter (Matt 27:7, 10; Rom 9:21).

Greek pēlos (G4081) — clay (John 9:6, 11, 14-15 of the clay Christ made with spittle; Rom 9:21).

Usage

"We are the clay, and thou our potter; and we all are the work of thy hand—Isa 64:8’s confession of the LORD’s sovereign forming."

"Hath not the potter power over the clay, of the same lump to make one vessel unto honour, and another unto dishonour?—Rom 9:21’s structural defense of God’s sovereign election."

"Universalist-Arminian reading mutes Rom 9’s substantive doctrine; hyper-Calvinist reading loses creaturely responsibility; biblical doctrine holds both: the LORD’s absolute sovereignty and the creature’s real responsibility as compatible truths."
